extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners who represent trademark applicants before the USPTO (trademark practitioners, OED counsel, and trademark law practices)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and sanctions governing practitioners who file and prosecute trademark applications before the USPTO, with emphasis on signature requirements, client communications, ethical duties, disciplinary procedures, suspension obligations, and reinstatement conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO signature requirement (personal entry)
rubrics_metrics.description: All documents must be personally signed. 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(a)(1), (c)(1), 11.18(a). The person(s) identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature. Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP §611.01(c) (Oct. 2018) explains that typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature. The USPTO requires the electronic signature to be entered at the time of filing so the signer personally verifies the facts at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations signed under penalty of perjury
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations in trademark applications are signed under penalty of perjury, with false statements subject to punishment under 18 U.S.C. § 1001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signatories make specific representations regarding use of the mark in commerce or intent to use; the USPTO relies on these representations in examination and issuance of registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEAS electronic signature timing and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: For trademark applications entered via TEAS, the electronic signature is required to be entered at the time of filing to ensure the signer personally verifies the facts set forth in the document at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must not allow others to enter their electronic signature into TEAS after the practitioner has returned a signed file; submission must reflect the signer’s contemporaneous verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to know who is the client
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner has an ethical obligation under the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct to know who is the client (Responsibilities of Practitioners Representing Clients in Proceedings Before the Patent and Trademark Office).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working through foreign intermediaries, the trademark applicant is the client, not the intermediary. See cited guidance and Srojirenstvi v. Toyoda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client identity when working with foreign intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a trademark practitioner works with a foreign intermediary, the client is the trademark applicant (the trademark owner), not the foreign agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A U.S. practitioner receiving instructions through a foreign agent does not change that the client is the trademark owner (1091 OG 26; Srojirenstvi v. Toyoda).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.101 — competent representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall provide competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101). Competence includes understanding who the client is, knowing USPTO trademark signature requirements, and personally certifying adequate review of specimens and reasonable inquiry supporting declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failures noted include: (i) not appreciating that the trademark applicants were her clients, (ii) misunderstanding that others signing her name on TEAS was impermissible, and (iii) not knowing the U.S. Counsel Rule/11.18(b)(2)(iii) required personal certification of specimen review and reasonable inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 — diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing clients (37 C.F.R. § 11.103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes taking reasonable steps to ensure clients’ trademark filings are signed in accordance with USPTO signature rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(2) — reasonable consultation about means
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall reasonably consult with the client about the means by which the client's objectives are to be accomplished (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner's duty includes notifying trademark applicants when signatures may be impermissible and advising about potential adverse consequences to IP rights; failure to notify violates this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) — keep client reasonably informed
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes informing clients when practitioner will no longer serve as local counsel; failing to inform after termination violates this duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b) — explain matter to permit informed decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must explain the significance of impermissible signatures and potential adverse consequences; failure to do so is a breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d) — protect client interests on termination
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must take reasonable measures to protect the interests of clients upon termination of representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligations include informing clients of termination and ensuring continuity/notification so client’s rights are protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1) — false statements / correcting false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall not knowingly make false statements of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct false statements previously made (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing others to sign the practitioner's name on trademark filings (including declarations) when the Office relies on those filings constitutes making/allowing false statements or failing to correct them.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(3) — offering false evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall not knowingly offer false evidence to a tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing declarations bearing the practitioner's signature when the practitioner did not personally sign/verify may be offering false evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(d) — disclosure of material facts to the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must inform the Office of all material facts known to the practitioner that will enable the Office to make an informed decision in an ex parte proceeding (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to disclose that others signed the practitioner's name on trademark applications is a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.304(c) — obedience to tribunal rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall not knowingly disobey an obligation under the rules of a tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.304(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing others to sign the practitioner's name to trademark documents in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 2.193 and/or § 2.11 is disobeying tribunal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.505 — assisting unauthorized practice of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall not assist another in practicing law in a jurisdiction in violation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction (37 C.F.R. § 11.505).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes failing to communicate directly with clients and permitting non-practitioners to counsel clients on substantive legal matters, allowing Entities to sign the practitioner's name, and using processes that cede control over final filings to non-practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d) — conduct prejudicial to administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include permitting non-practitioners to counsel clients, allowing others to sign practitioner’s name on documents the Office relies upon, and ceding filing control to non-practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (37 C.F.R. § 2.11) and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Counsel Rule requires applicants, registrants, or parties domiciled outside the U.S. to be represented by an attorney who is an active member in good standing of a U.S. state bar (84 FR 31498; 37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: increase compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations, improve accuracy of submissions, safeguard integrity of the trademark register. Practitioners are expected to undertake bona fide review of specimens and ensure accuracy of filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on typing another's electronic signature
rubrics_metrics.description: Typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature under USPTO rules (TMEP §611.01(c); supported by case law In re Dermahose Inc., In re Cowan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Just as signing another's name on paper is not a valid signature, entering another's electronic signature into TEAS is invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction — suspension and probation terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreed sanction included six (6) months suspension from practice before the Office (commencing 14 days from the Final Order) and a probationary period of twelve (12) months after reinstatement (with provisions for ending after three years if no reinstatement sought).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probation includes a practice monitor requirement and conditions that allow additional suspension if probation terms or rules are violated. Respondent bears costs of monitor and must secure a monitor acceptable to OED (not related, not former client, not disciplined).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice monitor requirement and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent with any petition for reinstatement, the respondent must provide a letter from an attorney agreeing to serve as practice monitor for one year starting upon reinstatement; the monitor must submit reports to the OED Director every three months certifying awareness of Respondent's practice and conformity with USPTO Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice monitor may not be related to respondent, previously engaged in an attorney-client relationship with respondent, or have been disciplined by USPTO or other jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and public notice of disciplinary action
rubrics_metrics.description: OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order at OED’s FOIA Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public notice includes identifying violations, suspension/probation terms, and factual summary of misconduct and corrective actions taken by respondent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations during suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended practitioner must: not render legal advice/services before the Office; not hold out as authorized to practice; change/remove advertising; file notices of withdrawal in pending applications; provide written notice of suspension to jurisdictions and agencies of admission; provide notice to clients advising lack of authority and urgent dates; deliver client documents; relinquish client funds; notify opposing practitioners/parties; and serve notices by certified mail or delivery service with receipt confirmation (37 C.F.R. § 11.58).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For clients domiciled outside the U.S. (e.g., China), electronic communication with translated notice is permissible if respondent keeps records and can confirm delivery or obtains written confirmation from the client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of compliance under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 (content requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent must file an affidavit of compliance certifying compliance with suspension provisions and append proof of distribution of funds and closing of accounts; a schedule of bank accounts designated as client/trust/fiduciary accounts; a schedule describing disposition of client/fiduciary funds; a list of other jurisdictions of admission; and an affidavit describing steps taken to remove advertising implying authorization to practice before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendices to the affidavit must include copies of checks/instruments, forms of notice, names/addresses of recipients, and return receipts or other delivery confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition for reinstatement requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: After suspension and compliance with 11.58, respondent may file a petition for reinstatement under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60; the petition must be filed with OED, accompanied by required fee, comply with § 11.60(c)(1)-(3), and attest (sworn) to compliance including that respondent did not practice before the Office during suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent cannot resume practice until reinstated by order of the OED Director or USPTO Director; petition procedures and fees must be followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify clients and effectuate corrective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must notify clients if signatures on their trademark applications may be impermissible and take measures to correct applications (e.g., filing Voluntary Amendments, contacting clients, identifying affected applications to USPTO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to notify clients prior to complaint was cited as misconduct; remedial steps (severing relationships with referring entities, contacting clients, submitting lists to USPTO) are mitigating considerations.
